nodes.title: Google Kubernetes Engine: Key Ideas
nodes.content: GKE is GCP's managed Kubernetes service — two flavors: Standard (you manage node pools) and Autopilot (Google manages nodes, you only pay for pod resources). Exam questions test node pools, networking, identity, and which mode to pick.

flashcards.front: GKE Standard vs Autopilot — which to pick?
flashcards.back: Standard: you create and size node pools, pay for nodes whether pods use them or not, full control. Autopilot: Google sizes nodes automatically, you pay only for pods' CPU/RAM/storage, hands-off but less flexibility (e.g., DaemonSets restricted). Pick Autopilot for new projects; Standard when you need GPUs, large nodes, or custom OS.

flashcards.front: What's a node pool?
flashcards.back: A group of nodes with the same machine type, OS, and config inside a GKE cluster. You can have multiple pools (e.g., default + gpu-pool + high-memory-pool). Pods can be scheduled to specific pools via node selectors or taints. Upgrades happen per pool, so prod and batch can be on different K8s versions.

flashcards.front: Workload Identity — why use it?
flashcards.back: Lets a Kubernetes Service Account impersonate a Google Cloud Service Account — pods get GCP IAM permissions without long-lived JSON keys. Replaces the dangerous pattern of mounting `gcp-sa-key.json` as a secret. Always-on by default in Autopilot; opt-in for Standard.

flashcards.front: VPC-native vs routes-based clusters.
flashcards.back: VPC-native: pods get IPs from a secondary range of your VPC — direct routing, no overlay overhead, supports private GKE. Routes-based: legacy, uses GCP routes table (limited to 200 routes per VPC). All new clusters should be VPC-native; routes-based is for legacy compatibility only.

nodes.title: Networking fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Networking moves packets between machines using layered protocols (the OSI / TCP-IP stack). Most exam questions test routing decisions, subnetting math, the difference between L2 and L3, and how DNS / DHCP make the whole thing usable for humans.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between Layer 2 and Layer 3?
flashcards.back: L2 (data link) uses MAC addresses to deliver frames inside a single broadcast domain (a switch). L3 (network) uses IP addresses to route packets between networks (a router). Switches do L2; routers do L3.

flashcards.front: How does a subnet mask work?
flashcards.back: The mask splits an IP into a network portion (the high bits, set to 1) and a host portion (the low bits, set to 0). `/24` means the first 24 bits are network = up to 256 hosts (254 usable). `/30` is 4 IPs = 2 hosts — typical for a point-to-point link.

flashcards.front: What does DNS do?
flashcards.back: Domain Name System translates human-readable names (`example.com`) into IP addresses. A recursive resolver asks the root, the TLD server (`.com`), and finally the authoritative server for the domain. TTL controls how long answers are cached.

flashcards.front: TCP vs UDP — when do you pick each?
flashcards.back: TCP is reliable, ordered, congestion-controlled — use it when every byte matters (HTTP, SSH, SMTP). UDP is lightweight, no handshake, no retransmit — use it for streaming, gaming, DNS queries, anywhere latency beats reliability.

questions.q: You need to allow internet traffic on TCP port 443 to a fleet of VMs in your VPC. No firewall rule for port 443 exists yet. What must you do?
choices: Establish a VPC peering link to route inbound 443 traffic from the public internet
Assign each VM an external IP address and enable IP forwarding on the instances
Create an ingress firewall rule allowing TCP:443 from 0.0.0.0/0 to the target VMs
Deploy a Cloud NAT gateway and use it as an inbound HTTPS reverse proxy
questions.explanation: GCP VPCs apply an implicit deny-all on ingress, so you must create an explicit ingress firewall rule allowing TCP:443 from source 0.0.0.0/0 (typically scoped to target tags or service accounts). Assigning external IPs only gives instances internet addressability — it does not open any port through the firewall. Cloud NAT only provides source-NAT for outbound flows; it does not accept unsolicited inbound traffic. VPC peering connects two private VPCs and cannot peer with the public internet.

questions.q: A subnet hosts VMs with no public IPs that must reach the public internet for OS updates and SaaS APIs while remaining unreachable from inbound flows. You want a managed regional resource that source-NATs the outbound flows behind shared addresses. Which GCP resource fits?
choices: An external HTTP(S) Load Balancer in front of the subnet
Cloud Router with custom advertised routes
Cloud NAT attached to the VPC and region
questions.explanation: Cloud NAT performs source NAT for instances without external IP addresses, allowing outbound connections while accepting no unsolicited inbound traffic. Cloud Armor is an L7 WAF in front of HTTP(S) load balancers and does not provide outbound NAT. An external load balancer handles inbound traffic. Cloud Router exchanges BGP routes between a VPC and on-premises networks; it is required as the control plane for Cloud NAT but is not itself the NAT data plane.

questions.q: Which load balancer should you choose to route HTTP/HTTPS traffic globally to backends in multiple regions with built-in DDoS protection?
questions.explanation: The Global External HTTP(S) Load Balancer is a Layer 7 proxy on Google's global front-end that steers each request to the closest healthy backend across regions and integrates with Cloud Armor for WAF and DDoS protection. Internal load balancers only serve clients inside the VPC. Regional external balancers terminate in a single region and cannot route across regions natively.

questions.q: You need to connect your on-premises network to a GCP VPC with dedicated 10 Gbps bandwidth, low latency and a service-level agreement. Which connectivity option fits?
choices: Cloud VPN over the public internet using IPsec tunnels
Cloud NAT with a private routing table to on-premises
Partner Interconnect through a supported service provider
Dedicated Interconnect via cross-connect in a Google colocation facility
questions.explanation: Dedicated Interconnect provides a direct physical fibre cross-connect between your on-premises router (in a Google colocation facility) and Google's edge network. It supports 10 Gbps or 100 Gbps circuits with a 99.9% SLA (99.99% with the recommended redundant topology). Cloud VPN traverses the public internet and offers no bandwidth SLA. Partner Interconnect uses a service-provider link with bandwidth options below or above 10 Gbps but is a managed-partner topology, not a direct cross-connect. Cloud NAT is an outbound-only service.

questions.q: Which GCP service caches HTTP(S) content at Google's global edge locations for backends behind the external HTTP(S) Load Balancer?
questions.explanation: Cloud CDN integrates with the Global External HTTP(S) Load Balancer to cache content at Google's edge points of presence, reducing latency for end users and origin load. Cloud Armor protects the same load balancer with WAF and DDoS controls but does not cache. Cloud Endpoints manages API contracts and gateway behaviour, not edge caching. Traffic Director is a managed service-mesh control plane for east-west service traffic.

questions.q: You are creating a custom VPC network for a new project and choose 'Custom' subnet mode. What does this setting mean?
choices: GCP automatically creates one /20 subnet in each region inside the VPC
No subnets are created automatically; you define each subnet's region and CIDR range manually
The VPC enables IPv6 addressing by default on every subnet you create in it
Custom mode allows overlapping IP ranges with other VPCs in the same project
questions.explanation: In Custom subnet mode the VPC ships with no subnets; you define each subnet's region and CIDR range manually, giving full control over IP planning. In Auto mode GCP creates one /20 subnet per region with predefined ranges. Custom is recommended for production to avoid IP overlaps that would block future VPC peering or hybrid connectivity. Subnet mode does not toggle IPv6 and does not change how IP overlap is detected with other VPCs.

nodes.title: Order the GCP resource hierarchy

data.scenario: Arrange the GCP resource hierarchy from the root (top) down to where resources live.

nodes.explanation: Google Cloud nests resources: the Organization is the root, Folders group projects, Projects hold the actual resources. IAM policies set higher up are inherited downward.

nodes.title: Identity and access management: Key Ideas
nodes.content: IAM is the layer that decides who can do what. It's almost always the first thing to misconfigure and the most common security failure mode. Every cloud uses the same primitives — identities, policies, roles — under slightly different names.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between authentication and authorization?
flashcards.back: Authentication (AuthN) proves who you are — password, MFA, certificate. Authorization (AuthZ) decides what you're allowed to do once authenticated — policies, roles, ACLs. AuthN happens first; AuthZ is checked on every request.

flashcards.front: What is a role (vs a user)?
flashcards.back: A user is a long-lived identity tied to a person. A role is a short-lived, assumable identity — services or users 'become' the role to get temporary credentials. Roles let you grant access without sharing long-term keys. Always prefer roles.

flashcards.front: Identity-based vs resource-based policies.
flashcards.back: Identity-based policies attach to a user / role and say what THEY can do. Resource-based policies attach to a thing (S3 bucket, KMS key, SQS queue) and say who can access IT. Cross-account access usually needs both: target's resource policy says 'allow this account', source identity policy says 'allow this action on that resource'.

flashcards.front: Why federation / SSO?
flashcards.back: Instead of creating cloud users for every employee, federate from your corporate identity provider (Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace). Users sign in once with their work account; the IdP issues a SAML / OIDC token; the cloud trades it for temporary credentials. One source of truth, instant deprovisioning.

questions.q: A developer needs to grant a service account the minimum permissions to read objects from a specific Cloud Storage bucket. Which IAM role should be granted at the bucket level?
questions.explanation: roles/storage.objectViewer grants storage.objects.get and storage.objects.list on the bucket's objects, satisfying read-only least privilege. roles/storage.objectCreator allows uploads only and does not grant read. roles/storage.objectAdmin adds write and delete on objects, far more than needed. roles/storage.legacyBucketReader grants metadata read on the bucket itself but does not grant access to read the object data.

questions.q: You are creating a Compute Engine VM that must call BigQuery and Cloud Storage APIs without any credential file stored on disk. What is the recommended approach?
choices: Copy a JSON service-account key onto the VM disk and load it from the application
Set the service-account credentials in startup-script environment variables
Attach a dedicated service account to the VM and grant it the required roles
Use the default Compute Engine service account with the project Editor role
questions.explanation: Attach a dedicated service account to the VM. Workloads on the VM authenticate to Google Cloud APIs by retrieving short-lived access tokens from the instance metadata server — no key file is required. Storing a JSON key on the disk creates a long-lived credential at risk of theft or accidental commit. Putting the key in startup-script env vars is equivalent to disk storage and is logged. The default compute service account with project Editor is over-privileged and violates least privilege.

questions.q: An admin wants to grant an IAM role to every member of their Google Workspace organisation in a single binding — employees, contractors and future hires alike — without having to maintain a group. Which principal identifier should they reference on the binding?
questions.explanation: The `domain:DOMAIN_NAME` principal grants the role to every Google account in the named Google Workspace or Cloud Identity domain, with no group to manage. `allUsers` grants access to anyone on the internet including unauthenticated callers — far too broad. `allAuthenticatedUsers` covers any Google-authenticated user globally, not just your company. `group:` requires that an actual Google Group exist and be populated with the right members; it is not the domain-wide identifier.

questions.q: You need to give an external auditor read-only access to every Cloud Logging entry in a project, including Data Access audit logs. What is the minimum predefined IAM role that satisfies this?
questions.explanation: roles/logging.privateLogViewer grants read access to all log entries including Data Access audit logs, which are treated as private. roles/logging.viewer only exposes Admin Activity and System Event audit logs and would hide Data Access entries. roles/viewer is a broad project-level read role that exceeds least privilege. roles/logging.admin grants full control over Cloud Logging — sinks, configuration and deletion — which is far more than read-only.

questions.q: You need to give a VM in Project A access to a Cloud Storage bucket in Project B. What is the correct, least-privileged approach?
choices: Cross-project access is blocked by default; open a quota or support ticket to permit it
Share Project A owner credentials with a service account in Project B
Grant the VM's service account the required role on the bucket in Project B
Establish VPC Network Peering between Project A and Project B networks
questions.explanation: IAM bindings can name any principal — including a service account from another project — on any resource. Grant the VM's service account the role it needs (for example `roles/storage.objectViewer`) on the specific bucket in Project B. Cross-project IAM is the standard, supported pattern; no quota change or peering is required. Sharing owner credentials is a serious anti-pattern that violates account ownership. VPC peering connects networks but does not authorise IAM access to a bucket.

nodes.title: GCP managed database services: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Google Cloud provides managed databases spanning relational, NoSQL, and globally distributed models. GCP ACE exams test which service fits a given workload and the key trade-offs.

flashcards.front: Cloud SQL vs Cloud Spanner — key difference?
flashcards.back: Cloud SQL: managed MySQL/PostgreSQL/SQL Server for regional workloads. Cloud Spanner: globally distributed, strongly consistent, horizontally scalable — no regional limit.

flashcards.front: Firestore vs Bigtable — choose by workload?
flashcards.back: Firestore: document/NoSQL for mobile and web apps with rich queries and real-time sync. Bigtable: wide-column store for high-throughput time-series or IoT data (no rich queries).

flashcards.front: Cloud Memorystore — what runtimes does it support?
flashcards.back: Managed Redis and Memcached — fully compatible with open-source clients, no patching required, used for caching and session storage.

flashcards.front: When would you choose AlloyDB over Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL?
flashcards.back: AlloyDB is Google's PostgreSQL-compatible database optimised for analytical and transactional mixed workloads; faster than standard Cloud SQL for HTAP use cases.

questions.q: You need a fully managed relational database service on GCP that is wire-compatible with MySQL 8.0. Which product should you choose?
questions.explanation: Cloud SQL is Google's fully managed relational database service and offers MySQL (5.6/5.7/8.0), PostgreSQL and SQL Server engines — applications can connect with standard MySQL drivers. Cloud Spanner is a globally distributed relational database but uses its own SQL dialect and is not wire-compatible with MySQL. Cloud Bigtable is a wide-column NoSQL store. Firestore is a document-oriented NoSQL database with no relational schema.

questions.q: You need to store structured, schemaless JSON documents with real-time sync for a mobile application. Which GCP database is the best fit?
questions.explanation: Firestore in Native mode is Google's serverless document database with native real-time listeners, offline persistence on mobile/web SDKs and automatic horizontal scaling — purpose-built for mobile and web apps. Cloud Bigtable is a wide-column store for analytics and high-throughput time-series workloads, with no document model or real-time listeners. Cloud SQL and Cloud Spanner are relational databases requiring a fixed schema and do not provide live mobile sync.

questions.q: A Cloud SQL primary is hot on read traffic. You want to offload read-only queries without rewriting the application's data layer. What should you add?
choices: Upgrade the primary instance to a larger machine type
Migrate the workload to Cloud Spanner for horizontal read scale-out
Add Memorystore for Redis in front as a read-through cache
Add a Cloud SQL read replica and point read traffic at its connection string
questions.explanation: Cloud SQL read replicas are asynchronously replicated copies of the primary that serve read-only queries. The application just connects to the replica's connection string for reads — no schema or SQL-dialect changes. Upgrading the primary helps but still uses a single instance and is more expensive. Memorystore requires application-level cache code and cache-invalidation handling. Migrating to Spanner is a major schema and SQL-dialect change, not a quick offload.

questions.q: You need to migrate a 5 TB PostgreSQL database from on-premises to Cloud SQL with continuous replication and minimal cutover downtime. Which GCP service is purpose-built for this?
questions.explanation: Database Migration Service (DMS) provides managed, low-downtime migrations from MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server and Oracle to Cloud SQL and AlloyDB. It performs an initial dump and then continuous logical replication, so cutover takes minutes. Cloud Dataflow runs general-purpose Apache Beam pipelines and is not a managed DB-to-DB replicator. Cloud Data Fusion is visual ETL/ELT for analytics, not OLTP migration. Transfer Appliance is for offline bulk file transfer, not live database replication.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.
